paras: I write today regarding the industrial overcapacity of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and its dumping of goods into U.S. markets, which systematically distort fair market competition, destabilize U.S. industries, and threaten domestic manufacturers and workers. The effects of the PRC’s overcapacity extend far beyond individual sectors—affecting the broader U.S. economy and undermining entire supply chains. There is a clear connection between falling PRC capacity utilization and increased production capacity that when paired with declining domestic prices puts downward pressure on prices outside the PRC. The artificial depression of prices by oversupply calls for adjustments in the cost structures submitted by these foreign producers.1 These dynamics lead to PRC products flooding global markets with underpriced products, actively eroding the competitiveness internationally and particularly for American businesses. This trend disrupts fair pricing mechanisms, encourages overinvestment in unsustainable production, and forces foreign producers to rely heavily on exports—often at the expense of U.S. manufacturers. Compounded by government subsidies and opaque pricing structures, the PRC’s overproduction has resulted in artificially low prices both in the U.S. and global markets.

As I evaluate the damaging effects of PRC overcapacity, I believe it is critical that as part of its analysis in antidumping investigations, the Department of Commerce (Commerce) should apply the special rules for costs under 19 U.S.C. § 1677b(f)(1)(A) more broadly. By adopting these rules, Congress empowered Commerce to adjust reported costs when they do not reasonably reflect the costs associated with the production and sale of subject merchandise. Given the PRC’s widespread overcapacity and the subsequent market distortions, I believe that 1 Thomas Gatley, Unpacking China’s Excess Capacity, GAVEKAL DRAGONOMICS (June 14, 2024), available at: https://research.gavekal.com/teaser/unpacking-chinas-excess-capacity/.

Page 2 of 5 this provision should be applied rigorously to ensure that the costs submitted by foreign producers do not unfairly skew antidumping calculations. The ability of foreign producers to underreport costs, particularly when these are distorted by PRC government subsidies and overproduction, undermines the fairness of U.S. trade laws.

The epoxy resin industry provides a clear case study of how PRC overcapacity and dumping practices are impacting U.S. industry. Below, I will present six key quantitative measures that demonstrate the harmful effects of these practices on U.S. producers as a way of defining PRC overcapacity and dumping. As these examples show, market-distorting practices in the PRC result in dumped and subsidized imports from that country, and those practices also distort markets – and contribute to unfair trade – in other countries. It is vital that Commerce use all the tools Congress has given it to address this challenge. Not only do I believe the evidence strongly supports a deeper inquiry by Commerce —both under the special rules for costs and other trade remedy provisions—but also that these quantitative measures can be used as a tool for other industries as well.

1. Falling Utilization of Existing Capacity As you know, capacity utilization is a key indicator of industry health. The U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC), in its recent preliminary determinations, has documented a substantial decline in capacity utilization between 2021 and 2023 by foreign epoxy resin producers. This decline reflects a broader trend of falling production levels in the face of foreign competition, specifically from PRC and other countries’ imports that are distorted by the PRC’s overcapacity and are sold at prices below fair market value. The ITC found that domestic production and capacity utilization rates dropped as PRC and other producers aggressively undersold U.S. manufacturers—gaining market share and depressing prices. In a competitive market, when domestic capacity utilization declines production capacity would fall in response. However, in the PRC market, domestic capacity utilization has instead led to an expansion of production capacity, further driving down domestic and global prices—a clear indication of PRC overcapacity.

Furthermore, foreign producers—including those in the PRC, India, South Korea, Taiwan, and Thailand—reported declining capacity utilization from 78.4% in 2021 to 71.4% in 2023. Despite their falling utilization rates, these producers continued to expand their capacity, flooding the U.S. market with excess product. Given these facts, I believe it is important for Commerce to apply the special rules for costs, because the reported costs of these foreign producers likely fail to reflect the true costs of production under normal market conditions. Indeed, overcapacity in the PRC appears to be a major driver of distorted costs outside the PRC. The artificial depression of prices by oversupply calls for adjustments in the cost structures submitted by these foreign producers.

Producers from the PRC and other countries expanded their capacity from 2.65 billion pounds in 2021 to over 3.23 billion pounds projected by 2025. This overinvestment in new capacity far exceeds justified demand and puts U.S. producers at a permanent disadvantage, as they are forced to bypass necessary investments to stay competitive. Applying the special rules for costs would allow Commerce to account for this overinvestment, which is driven by distorted pricing and overproduction rather than real market demand.

Overcapacity is amplified by unsustainable levels of fixed-asset investment in new production capacity. Between 2021 and 2023, U.S. producers saw their capital investments and research and development (R&D) expenses decline—largely due to the pressure of low-priced imports. The ITC found that domestic producers, despite strong demand, were unable to justify new investments because of unfair competition from abroad.

The epoxy resin industry is particularly vulnerable to foreign producers who are increasingly dependent on exports to manage their overcapacity. From 2021 to 2023, U.S. producers saw a decline in both the volume and value of their export sales, while foreign producers became more dependent upon exports, with shipments to the U.S. market rising from 8.4% of their total shipments in 2021 to 10.3% of their total shipments in 2023. These trends demonstrate that foreign producers are using the U.S. market to offload excess production, exacerbating the challenges faced by U.S. manufacturers.

Given that foreign producers are heavily reliant on exports to maintain high levels of production, the special rules for costs must be applied in a manner ensuring that costs reported by these producers reflect market conditions that would exist absent the distortions caused by overcapacity. Without such adjustments, foreign producers can and will manipulate their cost structures to evade responsibility under U.S. trade laws – thereby thwarting the intent of Congress.

The ITC has also documented a significant decline in prices within the U.S. epoxy resin market. Between 2021 and 2023, the average unit values and net sales of U.S. producers dropped, in large part due to aggressive price competition from Chinese and other foreign producers. The falling prices in the domestic market have further eroded the competitiveness of U.S. manufacturers, as they are forced to sell at unsustainable levels to compete with artificially low-priced imports. These facts underscore the importance of Commerce’s using all its Congressionally mandated authority to address dumping by foreign producers. Action must be

The pricing pressure faced by U.S. producers is not limited to the domestic market. Between 2021 and 2023, the average unit values of U.S. export sales declined as well. The unit value of U.S. imports of epoxy resins from the PRC dropped by 22.2%, while the unit value of imports from all subject countries fell by 28%. These falling prices plainly result from foreign producers’ overcapacity, which forces them to sell at below-market prices to maintain production levels.

The special rules for costs should be applied to account for these price distortions. The reported export prices from the PRC and other countries do not reflect the true cost of production and sale when considering the market conditions caused by overcapacity. Commerce must ensure that the cost structures submitted by foreign producers are properly adjusted to prevent these distortions from further damaging U.S. industries.

The combined effects of falling prices and increased competition from underpriced imports have caused a significant decline in profit margins for U.S. epoxy resin producers. Between 2021 and 2023, U.S. producers experienced falling operating income, operating margins, and net income, as documented by the ITC. These trends are unsustainable and put the future of the U.S. epoxy resin industry at risk. The application of the special rules for costs is critical in this context, as foreign producers’ costs must be recalculated to reflect market conditions distorted by Chinese overcapacity. * * *

It is important to note that the overcapacity issues I highlight today are not limited to the epoxy resin industry. The PRC’s overcapacity in key chemical and industrial sectors, such as epichlorohydrin (ECH) and bisphenol A (BPA), has similarly led to a flood of subsidized products entering the global market. For example, between 2019 and 2023, the PRC ramped up its capacity for ECH, leading to further production of epoxy resins both in the PRC and in other countries in the region that are now being dumped into the U.S. market.

In this broader context, it is critical for Commerce to apply the special rules for costs to ensure that antidumping calculations accurately reflect the true costs of production. PRC overcapacity distorts global supply chains and allows foreign producers to evade the full force of U.S. trade laws. Without adjustments under these statutory provisions, U.S. industries will
